title: What the circus side-show band played; Harry James
summary: Circus music was fast ding-a-ling tunes with no reading, and Joe recalls Harry James's father leading a circus band.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: It seems to me that you weren't playing what you'd call Jazz in any of these things, right?
No, in a circus you didn't play nothing...really.
Some of it was ding-a-ling music to bring people into the show, almost like a medicine show.
What, did you have to read it?

You didn't read nothin'. We played some fast little thing, "Washington-and-Lee Swing, Baby," or something like that, or "Over The Waves" real fast. Everything was fast. But then you would play a better sort of number, because some guy had to sing...
You mean somebody on the show?

"The Robert E. Lee," [SINGS REFRAIN] they'd sing it, and a couple of old gals kicking their legs up in the air and dancing. And that was it. The circus was a real hokey thing. It was really the side-show. It wasn't an easy job to get in the Big Top. In fact, I wasn't a cap[able enough musician at the time to play a revue...to play in the circus, some of the hardest music there is.
Did any of the more, shall we say, famous musicians, famous now... Did any of them come through the circus bands?

Not as I... Now, Harry James at one time was on a circus. Harry James was born on a circus. They had a circus out of Galveston, Texas, called the Christy Brothers, and his father was a leader. In fact, his Dad used to come to the (?) room and jam with us. So did Harry. But Harry was on this circus.
